body.heading: A tiny puzzle
paragraphs: English speakers say 'on the bus' but 'in the car'. Why? Both are vehicles! There is a real rule hiding underneath, and once you see it, you will get it right nearly every time.
Read the rule, then test yourself on the sentences.

body.heading: The rule: can you stand up inside?
paragraphs: If the vehicle is big enough to stand up and walk around in, we say ON: on the bus, on the train, on the airplane, on the ship, on the ferry.
If the vehicle is small and you sit down inside it, we say IN: in the car, in the taxi, in the van, in the truck cab.
And if you sit on top and straddle it, we also say ON: on the bicycle, on the motorcycle, on the horse.

body.heading: Practice sentences
paragraphs: We got on the train at the station.
Dad is sitting in the car.
She is riding on her bicycle.
The passengers are on the airplane.
We traveled in a taxi to the beach.
He is traveling on a ship.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. A canoe: do you get in it or on it? (Trick question — most people say IN a canoe, because you sit down inside it.)
2. Invent a vehicle of the future. Would you ride in it or on it? Use the stand-up test to decide.

takeaway: Stand-up vehicles take 'on' (bus, train, plane, ship); sit-inside vehicles take 'in' (car, taxi, van); sit-on-top rides take 'on' too (bicycle, motorcycle).
